WHY IT HAS TO EXIST

The digital age has a language policy.
Nobody voted for it.

Market size decides which languages get AI. The result is a quiet sorting of the world’s languages into those with a digital future and those without.

F·01

Coverage is a rounding error

Around 249 languages on Google Translate, out of roughly 7,000 spoken. Researcher András Kornai estimated fewer than 5% of languages are ascending into digital use at all; the rest are digitally static or sinking.

F·02

Europe is not exempt

The META-NET studies rated 21 of 30 European languages as having weak or no support in key language-technology areas. Maltese, an official EU language, scored in the lowest band in every category studied.

F·03

Endangerment is accelerating

UNESCO estimates around 40% of the world’s languages are endangered. Digital absence compounds it: a language your phone cannot speak is a language your children practise less.

F·04

Small corpora, small priority

Maltese has real academic resources (the Korpus Malti runs to hundreds of millions of tokens, and local models like BERTu exist), but big-tech platform investment follows big markets. Underserved is the precise word.

META-NET: 21 OF 30 EUROPEAN LANGUAGES RATED WEAK OR UNSUPPORTED. MALTESE LOWEST IN EVERY CATEGORY
WHO IT SERVES

For the speakers,
and the language itself.

Maltese, the home case

VF Empire is a Maltese company. The national language of our own jurisdiction (semitic root, latin script, an official EU language) sits in the lowest support band of European language technology. We build for Maltese first because it is ours, and because if the methods work here they port to other underserved languages.

OFFICIAL EU LANGUAGELOWEST SUPPORT BANDOUR OWN HOMEMETHODS THAT PORT

Everyday speakers

Translation and writing assistance that treats the language as a first-class citizen: drafting, correcting and translating with real fluency.

Learners & the diaspora

Emigrant families and second-generation speakers get a serious learning tool, the bridge back to a language that classrooms abroad do not teach.

Institutions & media

Government, courts, broadcasters and publishers working under official bilingualism get language tooling that carries the load in both languages.

Language communities beyond Malta

The programme is a template: corpus tooling, training recipes and product patterns designed to be reapplied wherever a community wants its language to have a digital future.

WHAT IT CHANGES

From corpus
to living tools.

Preservation that matters is daily usefulness. The measure of the programme is whether speakers reach for the language more because the tools work.

Translation that respects.

Maltese–English and Maltese–EU-language translation built on and evaluated against real corpora, with fluency judged by native speakers.

Learning that connects.

A learner experience built from the corpus outward (real usage, real register, real voice) for students, diaspora and new residents alike.

A corpus that compounds.

Community-contributed text and speech, properly licensed and credited, growing the shared foundation future Maltese tools will stand on.

THE MECHANICS

Modern methods,
pointed at a small language.

Low-resource NLP is a real research field with real techniques: transfer learning, data-efficient fine-tuning, community corpus building. The programme applies them with engineering seriousness, building on the academic work Malta has already done.

LAYER 1

The corpus layer

Building on existing resources (the Korpus Malti tradition, public text, licensed archives) plus community contribution pipelines for text and speech, with clear licensing and credit.

LAYER 2

The model core

Data-efficient training: multilingual transfer, fine-tuning on curated Maltese data, evaluation sets built with native speakers. Standing on prior local work such as BERTu.

LAYER 3

The tool layer

Translation, writing assistance, speech interfaces and the learning product: the corpus made useful in daily life, which is what keeps it growing.

LAYER 4

The template layer

Everything documented as a repeatable method, so the second language costs a fraction of the first and communities can bring their own.
